confirmed: The source is the 15-page Frontiers in Psychology journal article published 02 July 2025; its title and five authors match the form (PDF p. 1 and PDF page count). The entire markdown conversion was read, including the end matter and references; the separate online supplement is linked on p. 14 and is not included in the PDF or reviewed here, consistent with source.version.

Section 3.1 explicitly states that participants were randomly assigned to the experimental group (n = 32; 17 females, 15 males) or control group (n = 32; 16 females, 16 males), supporting has_randomized_people_study = true and individual between-group assignment despite the contradictory quasi-experimental label in section 3.2.1 (PDF p. 4).

The controlled multimedia classroom in the university Design Innovation Laboratory supports lab_rct; context_class = none is appropriate for this people-assistance experiment (PDF p. 4, section 3.2.2; p. 5, section 3.2.3).

The study randomized 64 third-year undergraduate design students, 32 per arm, and Table 1 analyzes 32 per arm, 64 total; these are people rather than ideas, designs, or expert ratings, so the study exceeds the 50-person threshold (PDF p. 4, section 3.1; p. 7, section 3.7; p. 8, Table 1).

Participants came from Product Design and Visual Communication Design programs at a public university in Eastern China, were enrolled in a Design Innovation course, and lacked prior formal AIGC design training (PDF p. 4, section 3.1).
The task was to design an intelligent walking cane within 3 h and submit design sketches, three-dimensional models, and rendered images (PDF p. 6, section 3.4.1).

The experimental tools were ChatGPT, Midjourney, and Stable Diffusion; the described workflow combines ChatGPT ideation, Stable Diffusion image generation, and conventional image post-processing. Controls used internet research and conventional design software without AIGC; Midjourney use is also described in an interview quotation (PDF p. 4, section 3.2.2; p. 6, sections 3.4.2-3.4.3; p. 11, Table 3).

Three design experts independently scored participants' actual creative works using the Creative Solution Diagnosis Scale, supporting expert_raters, overall_creativity, scored_on_output = true, and with_ai; EEG concentration and relaxation are separate measures rather than creativity scores on the output (PDF pp. 5-6, sections 3.2.3 and 3.3.1-3.3.2).
The creativity means, SDs, and analyzed Ns are exactly experimental M = 115.13, SD = 6.440, N = 32 and control M = 110.69, SD = 9.372, N = 32 (PDF p. 8, Table 1, verified with PDF table extraction).

The creativity mean difference is 4.438 with 95% confidence interval [0.419, 8.456] (PDF p. 9, Table 2, verified with PDF table extraction); t(62) = 2.208 and p = 0.031 are stated in the prose (PDF p. 8, section 3.7; p. 11, section 4.1), and Cohen's d = 0.55 is explicitly reported (PDF p. 11, section 4.1). These also confirm every number in one_line_finding.

Table 2 actually places 2.208 beneath df and 62 beneath t; the form correctly discloses the reversed headings and uses the explicit prose to identify the statistic and degrees of freedom (PDF p. 9, Table 2; p. 8, section 3.7; p. 11, section 4.1).
The main article reports one experiment rather than a synthesis, so the default synthesis fields are appropriate (PDF pp. 4-8, sections 3.1-3.7; p. 13, section 6 describes a single design session).

The original short-form instructions deliberately require eligibility.core = unclear when random assignment is met or unclear, at least 50 people are analyzed, and an outcome is scored on the output; the form follows that referral rule and should proceed to the two-screener pipeline (codex-jobs/lscreen-c619/brief.md, SHORT-version eligibility bullet; supporting study evidence: PDF pp. 4-6 and p. 8, Table 1).
summary: The form's design, participant counts, and reported creativity statistics match the journal PDF. This is a randomized people study with 64 analyzed participants that should enter the two-screener pipeline, despite the paper's inconsistent quasi-experimental label.
